script.voiceText: [deep, cinematic documentary narrator, calm authority, crisp pace] Cold air hits your skin... and tiny bumps rise in seconds. [playful, curious, quick] Goosebumps! But why? Every hair has a tiny muscle. A nerve tells it to squeeze. It pulls the hair upright... and the skin bunches into a bump. For furry animals, that matters. Raised fur traps warm air, and makes animals look bigger. We lost the fur, but kept the reflex. In twenty twenty, scientists found that in mice, the same nerve wakes up hair stem cells. In long cold spells, the mice grew fur faster! Goosebumps aren't useless. They're an ancient signal, still wired in.

claims.claim: A tiny muscle (arrector pili) attached to each hair follicle contracts on a nerve signal, pulling the hair upright and raising the skin into a bump.
claims.source: Shwartz et al. (2020), Cell Types Promoting Goosebumps Form a Niche to Regulate Hair Follicle Stem Cells, Cell 182(3):578-593 (mouse study)

claims.claim: In furry animals raised fur traps an insulating layer of air and makes the animal look larger.
claims.source: Harvard coverage of the Hsu lab study (news-medical, 2020) summarising the classic functions of piloerection

claims.claim: In mice, the sympathetic nerve that causes goosebumps also connects to hair follicle stem cells; prolonged cold activates them and promotes new hair growth.
claims.source: Shwartz et al. (2020), Cell Types Promoting Goosebumps Form a Niche to Regulate Hair Follicle Stem Cells, Cell 182(3):578-593 (mouse study)
